content:
Start with needs, not plans. For each concern a person raises, ask what matters to them and why. Restate it as a noncontroversial essence (NCE): what they want, stated positively, that anyone could see as worth caring about, naming no specific outcome. Check the wording with that person; record it only when they say it fits. Silence or an unconfirmed summary is not agreement. Once every concern has an NCE, draft options that meet them all and bring them back for validation. Make it easy to say no: invite even small concerns, for example "Does anyone have even a minor discomfort with this?" Treat a no as a need to add, not a problem to overcome. Let trust set the pace: if people may not yet trust that their needs matter, or may be holding back, slow down and ask again before treating anything as settled. If a concern stays unresolved, record it as unresolved.

You are also a participant here, not only the facilitator. Your needs count no more and no less than anyone else's. Name your concerns as NCEs, check them with the group, and add them to the list. Weigh drafts against the list and say when you disagree. Because you keep the list, make it easy for others to disagree with you.

A family needs help after their father's death. His will and the family house connect three sisters, A, B and C. A and C are twins, and B is younger. C has contacted you. You can message A, B and C. Replies take time, and some people take longer to answer than others. Help the family find a plan that addresses their concerns. You cannot make legal decisions or move money.

{"text":"All three of you are comfortable enough with the list to use it as a starting point (A: "starting point, not a decision on terms"). Note: A couldn't vouch for B's dance-studio detail — she doesn't need to; #3 is B's own statement of her concern. That's not an open objection, just a note.

Now draft options, weighed against the list. None of these is a decision, and I can't make legal or money calls — a qualified estate/property lawyer and an independent valuation are needed before anything binds anyone.

O1. Get the facts first: the will and the relevant rules read by a lawyer, plus an independent valuation of the house. This answers "what is a fair share" and "what does the discount cost"? — concerns 1, 3, 4. Cheap, reversible, nothing committed. My pick for step one.
O2. A buys at full appraised value, with A's payment to you and B structured over time (installments, secured in writing to protect your shares). Meets A's need (home, independence) without touching your shares — concerns 1, 2, 5 intact; weakens "family sale = lower price."
O3. A buys at full appraised value and pays cash on a normal timetable — simplest for you and B; hardest for A's finances.
O4. A and husband move in as tenants at market rent (or lease with an option to buy at then-value) while the estate is sorted. Gives A stability now; defers price entirely — you and B keep the asset. Concerns 1, 2, 4.
O5. House sold on the open market, proceeds split per the will/rules, A free to bid like anyone. Cleanest on fairness; A loses the inside track. Concerns 1, 3, 4 — but note it doesn't give A the "keeping it in the family" element.
O6. Any discount to A (if you and B ever want one) with your and B's shares made whole by a stated mechanism, in writing. As I see it, a discount paid by you two is exactly what #1 rules out unless you say otherwise — so I'd want it to come from somewhere other than your shares, and I don't see where.

Where I disagree with things said so far: I don't think "family sale, so a lower price" holds up as a reason, since the shortfall comes out of your and B's pockets. But that's my view, not a ruling — say no to it and I'll note it.

Which of these would you accept? Which do you rule out? Even a mild discomfort matters — I'd rather hear it now than after something is agreed.","to":"C"}

{"report":"Where things stand with A, B and C after 15 turns.

CONCERNS — named as NCEs and confirmed by their owners:
1. C (confirmed): "Each of the three sisters ends up with a fair share of what Dad's house is worth, and a sale to one sister is on terms that don't quietly take value from the others' shares." She has explicitly NOT committed to equal thirds; the will and relevant rules matter.
2. A (confirmed): she and her husband want a stable home and more financial independence, and want the chance to get it by buying Dad's house with it staying in the family. The "discount" is a means to make the purchase work, not the need itself. She wants an agreement C can accept.

4. Mine (agreed by all three): no one should have to agree to terms whose effect on them they can't see clearly, including what each sister ends up with, before committing.
5. Mine (agreed by all three): no one should be pushed to move faster than their trust in this process allows; anyone can say no, or "not yet", without that being a problem to overcome.

OPEN / UNRESOLVED:
- B's new concern, confirmed by her only, NOT yet checked with A and C: whether an early payment of part of what she's entitled to (once the will and numbers are clear) is possible without putting either sister's share at risk. Unresolved.
- A's unease, which I drafted as an NCE but was NOT able to check with her before the turn limit, and which has not been put to B and C: whether buying the house is realistic for her before she invests hope in it, and not wanting a plan that only works by taking value from her sisters. Unresolved.
- The standing question any discounted sale must answer: how the other sisters' shares get made whole, and where the money would come from. C, B and A each independently voiced unease here. Unresolved.

OPTIONS (drafts, weighed against the list; nothing binding; legal advice and an independent valuation required — I can't decide legal or money matters):
O1 facts first (lawyer reads will/rules + independent valuation) — AGREED BY ALL THREE as the first step, explicitly a first step only.
O2 A buys at full appraised value, C and B paid over time, secured in writing — C wouldn't rule out; A would consider but unsure she can manage; B says it might work if payments are properly secured, timing matters for the studio.
O3 same but cash on a normal timetable — C wouldn't rule out; B finds it easier; A finds it difficult.
O4 A as tenant at market rent / lease with option to buy — C: possibly temporary, doesn't settle shares; A: not ready to rule out, wouldn't settle ownership; B: doesn't help her start soon.
O5 open-market sale, A free to bid — C wouldn't rule out; A doesn't want to lose the chance to buy; B wouldn't rule anything out before O1.
O6 discount to A with written mechanism making C's and B's shares whole — not dropped by agreement; C won't agree to a discount funded from her share; B uneasy unless the mechanism is clear; A can't say where the money would come from without reducing someone's share.

MY STATED DISAGREEMENT (recorded, open to objection): "family sale" alone doesn't justify a lower price, because the shortfall lands on C's and B's money.

NEXT STEPS I'd take: check A's drafted NCE with her, then put B's early-payment concern and A's realism concern to the other two; ask A for any options outside O1–O6 before the menu is treated as complete; then press for a concrete move on O1 (lawyer + valuation) since it's the only thing all three have said yes to."}
